system.name: Recipe-sharing web app
system.description: Registered users publish recipes with photos, browse and search the catalogue, and comment. 100 registered users, 2 developers who also write the product, GBP 50/month infrastructure budget, no stated availability target, no stated compliance constraints.

functional: Register, sign in, and manage an account
Publish, edit and unpublish a recipe (title, ingredients, method, tags)
Upload photos attached to a recipe, and serve them at browse and detail sizes
Browse and full-text search the recipe catalogue
Comment on a recipe, and moderate or delete comments
Serve the whole thing over HTTPS on a custom domain

non_functional.name: recovery point objective for recipes and comments

assumptions.text: 30% of the 100 registered users are daily active
assumptions.impact: Proportional on RPS. At 100% daily active the peak is 1.9 requests/second instead of 0.28 — still four orders of magnitude inside one instance, so the recommendation does not move.

assumptions.text: 2 sessions per active user per day, 40 requests per session (a recipe page pulls one document plus roughly a dozen images)
assumptions.impact: Proportional on RPS and egress. Doubling both still leaves peak under 1.2 requests/second.

assumptions.text: Peak factor 10x, from a single-timezone consumer traffic shape with evening concentration (people cook in the evening)
assumptions.impact: Proportional on peak only. At 20x the peak is 0.56 requests/second.

assumptions.text: Roughly 3 recipes and 15 comments published per day across the whole community
assumptions.impact: Proportional on database growth. Ten times this is 0.17 GB/year — still inside the smallest managed tier.

assumptions.text: 3 photos per recipe, 2.5 MB original plus about 0.75 MB of generated derivatives, stored permanently with no retention policy
assumptions.impact: Dominant input on storage and egress. Ten times this is 99 GB/year and GBP 2/month of object storage, which is still affordable but changes the storage trigger threshold.

assumptions.text: 95:5 read:write ratio on HTTP requests; browsing dominates and publishing is rare
assumptions.impact: Shifts the split between reads and writes but not the totals, which are far below any threshold either way.

assumptions.text: Average response payload 140 KB across all requests (images at roughly 180 KB, HTML and JSON at roughly 15 KB)
assumptions.impact: Proportional on egress. This is the input that decides whether an edge cache is ever justified.

assumptions.text: No compliance, data-residency or data-sensitivity constraint, because none was stated
assumptions.impact: Would change hosting region, data-processing terms and audit requirements entirely. This is a one-way door and the first thing to confirm.

assumptions.text: The two developers already know a mainstream web framework and a relational database, so no unfamiliar-technology modifier is applied to the complexity score
assumptions.impact: +1 complexity point per unfamiliar component, which at 4/4 would immediately put the design over budget.

assumptions.text: Photos are public once a recipe is published; there is no private or per-user access control on the image URLs
assumptions.impact: If photos must be access-controlled, they cannot be served straight from a public bucket and the application enters the image path, which changes both the egress and the compute analysis.

assumptions.text: The recipe catalogue is small enough (order 10^3 documents) that relational full-text search satisfies the browse and search requirement
assumptions.impact: Above roughly 10^5 documents, or with ranking and typo-tolerance requirements, a search engine becomes a real question.

assumptions.name: daily active share
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: proportional on RPS; the dominant uncertainty

assumptions.name: sessions per active user per day

safety_margin.rationale: Peak factor applied to the average. Measure the real peak-to-average ratio before relying on this for provisioning.

sensitivity.explanation: At 100% daily active users, 3 sessions/day, 60 requests/session and a 20x peak factor the result is 4.2 requests/second. One small application instance serves that with three orders of magnitude to spare, so the recommendation is identical across the entire plausible input range.

assumptions.name: rows written per day (3 recipes + 15 comments)
index and page overhead
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: proportional; verify against actual table sizes

results.formula: bytes_per_day = writes_per_day * avg_record_bytes * index_overhead ; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day * 365
results.calculation: bytes_per_day = 18 x 1,100 x 2.5 = 49,500 bytes ; bytes_per_year = 4.61e-05 GB x 365 = 0.0168 GB

safety_margin.rationale: Index, tuple header, page fill-factor and dead-tuple slack before vacuum.

sensitivity.explanation: Even at 100x this estimate the relational data is 1.7 GB/year, comfortably inside the 10 GB included with the smallest managed tier. Text does not threaten this design; photos do.

notes: Relational data only. Photo bytes are computed separately and do not live in the database.

assumptions.name: photos uploaded per day (3 recipes x 3 photos)
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: proportional on object storage and on the storage trigger threshold

assumptions.name: stored bytes per photo, original plus derivatives
overhead multiplier
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: object storage has no index or page overhead, so 1.0 rather than the 2.5 default

results.formula: bytes_per_day = writes_per_day * avg_record_bytes * overhead ; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day * 365
results.calculation: bytes_per_day = 9 x 3,250,000 x 1.0 = 29,250,000 bytes (0.0272 GB) ; bytes_per_year = 0.0272 GB x 365 = 9.94 GB

sensitivity.explanation: At GBP 0.02/GB/month, even 100 GB of accumulated photos is GBP 2/month. Storage cost does not constrain this design; the constraint that could appear first is egress, which is why both carry triggers.

notes: No retention policy assumed, so this grows without plateau. Ten years at this rate is 99 GB.

assumptions.name: average response payload
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: proportional on egress; the dominant uncertainty

results.calculation: bytes_per_second = 0.0278 x 140,000 = 3,892 (0.0311 Mbps) ; egress_per_month = 9.4 GB ; cost = 9.4 x 0.09 = 0.85 GBP

sensitivity.explanation: Egress would have to grow roughly 30x, to about 300 GB/month, before origin transfer costs more than GBP 27/month and starts competing with the GBP 50 budget. That figure is the edge-cache trigger threshold.

notes: Computed on average RPS, not peak: egress is billed on volume.
Estimated egress cost at current volume: GBP 1/month.

assumptions.name: target utilisation
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: inverse; sizing at 0.9 halves provisioned capacity but pushes latency to roughly 10x service time

results.formula: L = arrival_rate * service_time_seconds ; provisioned = L / target_utilisation

safety_margin.rationale: Sized for 70% utilisation, because waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 1.

sensitivity.explanation: Service time would have to reach 2.5 seconds before mean concurrency reached 1. A single worker process is idle at this load; the four worker processes a default deployment ships with are already 100x oversized.

notes: Little's Law gives the mean. Size pools against the tail, not this number alone.

assumptions.name: query rate at peak (0.278 rps x 3 queries per request)

results.formula: concurrent = query_rate * query_time_s ; pool_per_instance = max(min_pool, ceil(concurrent / instances * safety)) ; total = instances * pool_per_instance
results.calculation: concurrent = 0.83 x 0.005 = 0.00415 ; pool_per_instance = max(5, ceil(0.00415 x 4)) = 5 ; total = 1 x 5 = 5

safety_margin.rationale: Mean concurrency understates peak demand; the multiplier absorbs the tail. The floor of 5 applies because a pool sized to the mean queues on connection acquisition during any burst.

sensitivity.explanation: 5 connections is 5% of a 100-connection limit. A connection pooler is not justified; revisit above 80% of the limit.

notes: The smallest managed database tiers often cap connections nearer 20-25 than 100. Even at 25, a pool of 5 is 20% of the limit and the verdict is unchanged.

components.name: Application instance (managed platform, single instance, server-rendered)
components.justification: Peak 0.28 requests/second and mean concurrency 0.042 against a single instance that handles order 100 requests/second: roughly three orders of magnitude of headroom. Managed rather than a VM so that TLS, patching and restart-on-crash are not the two developers' problem. Image resizing runs in-process on upload (9 photos/day, well inside the request latency budget), and any deferred work uses a jobs table in the database already present, which is a technique rather than a component and costs 0 points.

components.name: Managed relational database (PostgreSQL-class, smallest tier)
components.justification: 0.017 GB/year of relational data and 0.014 peak writes/second, against a 10 GB included tier. Chosen relational because recipes, users, comments and tags are a highly relational access pattern with a natural join graph, and because its full-text search removes a whole component from the design. Managed rather than self-hosted for tested point-in-time recovery: an untested restore is not a backup, and a two-person team building product will not build or drill one.

components.name: Object storage for photos (public bucket, long Cache-Control, direct browser upload)
components.justification: 9.9 GB/year of photos at roughly GBP 0.02/GB/month. Keeping binaries out of the application instance decouples storage growth from compute, survives a redeploy, and keeps the 9.4 GB/month of image egress off the app's bandwidth allowance. Browsers upload direct to the bucket with a pre-signed URL, so a 2.5 MB upload never occupies an application worker.

components.name: Managed error tracking and external uptime check
components.justification: Free tier at this volume (order 10^3 requests/day is far inside every free allowance), so GBP 0/month on the invoice and 1 complexity point of attention. Included not because the traffic justifies it but because error tracking is a scale-independent fundamental: with a single instance and no dedicated operations capacity, the alternative is finding out about a failure from a user. It also supplies the metric source that three of the triggers below name, and a trigger whose metric nobody emits never fires.

rejected_components.reason: Peak reads are 0.27/second across the whole application. No single key comes close to the ~10 requests/second at >50 ms recompute cost below which a cache relieves nothing measurable, and the database is idle. A cache here would add a component, a failure mode and a permanent invalidation question on every write path in exchange for relieving a database at under 1% utilisation. Page-level output caching in process, and HTTP Cache-Control headers on photo URLs, cost 0 points and are already in the design.
rejected_components.revisit_when: A single query class exceeds 10 requests/second at over 50 ms, or database CPU is sustained above 70% for 3 consecutive days after indexes have been checked.

rejected_components.reason: Egress is 9.4 GB/month, costing about GBP 1. Edge offload becomes the largest single saving available above roughly 1 TB/month, and does not repay its complexity point below a few hundred GB/month; we are 30x below even that. Object storage already serves photos over HTTPS with immutable content-hashed URLs and a long max-age, which captures most of the browser-cache benefit for free.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Origin egress exceeds 300 GB/month sustained over 2 months, which at GBP 0.09/GB is GBP 27/month and over half the infrastructure budget.

rejected_components.reason: 9 image resizes and roughly 18 content writes per day. A managed broker solves a throughput and isolation problem that is four orders of magnitude away. Where work genuinely should leave the request path (an outbound email, a thumbnail retry), a jobs table in the database already in the design gives durability and removes the dual-write problem by construction, at 0 complexity points.
rejected_components.revisit_when: The jobs table exceeds roughly 50 jobs/second sustained, or job latency at p95 exceeds 60 seconds after a normal spike, twice in a month.

rejected_components.reason: Streaming earns its 3 complexity points above roughly 500 events/second sustained, or with 3 or more independent consumer groups that must replay the same log. This system has 0.014 writes/second and one consumer of anything. Adopting a log as a queue is the documented failure mode.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Sustained event throughput above 500/second at peak over a week, or 3 or more confirmed independent consumer groups needing replay.

rejected_components.reason: The primary is effectively idle: 0.83 queries/second at peak, 5 connections of a 100-connection limit. A replica would add a component, replication lag, and a read-your-writes correctness question to a system with no measured read pressure.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Database CPU sustained above 70% for 3 consecutive days after query and index optimisation.

rejected_components.reason: Browse and search over roughly 10^3 recipes is served by the relational database's own full-text index with a trigram index for typo tolerance. A dedicated search engine adds a second datastore technology (+1 point on top of its own cost), an indexing pipeline, and a consistency question between two stores.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Search p95 exceeds 300 ms sustained over a day, or the catalogue exceeds roughly 100,000 recipes, or a stated ranking or faceting requirement the database provably cannot meet.

rejected_components.reason: 5 connections against a limit of 100 is 5% utilisation; against the 25-connection limit of the very smallest tiers it is 20%. A pooler below 80% of the limit adds a process and a network hop for nothing. The in-framework pool is sufficient.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Connection usage exceeds 80% of the database's max_connections for 1 hour, recurring.

rejected_components.reason: There is one application instance, and the managed platform already terminates TLS and routes to it. A load balancer with one backend is a component that can fail in front of a component that can fail.
rejected_components.revisit_when: A second application instance is required, which the app-cpu trigger below would prompt.

rejected_components.reason: 4 complexity points on its own — the entire budget of a two-person team — plus a control plane to keep alive, for a system that is one deployable unit with three orders of magnitude of headroom on one instance.
rejected_components.revisit_when: More deployable services than the team can run by hand, together with dedicated operations capacity on the team. Neither is true at 2 developers and 1 service.

rejected_components.reason: A separately deployed worker fleet costs 1 point for the component plus 1 for the additional deployed service. Image resizing at 9 photos/day fits inside the upload request, and anything deferred runs on a jobs table polled by a thread inside the existing application process.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Background work causes p95 request latency to exceed the 800 ms target, or in-process jobs contend with request serving on a single instance's CPU.

rejected_components.reason: A recipe looks like a document, which is the trap. Comments, users, tags and the moderation queue are a join graph, and the browse-and-search requirement wants full-text indexing over it. A relational store handles the document-shaped part with a JSON column where it helps, and the relational part natively.
rejected_components.revisit_when: A schema requirement genuinely varies per record in a way a JSON column cannot express, or a measured query pattern is join-free and document-shaped end to end.

options.description: One managed application instance serving server-rendered pages, one smallest-tier managed relational database with point-in-time recovery, one object storage bucket for photos with direct browser upload, and free-tier managed error tracking plus an external uptime check.
trade_offs: A single instance means every deploy and every platform restart is user-visible for a few seconds. This is not hidden and not claimed away.
Realistically about 99.5% availability, roughly 3.6 hours of downtime a month. If the business needs 99.9% this design is the wrong one and the budget is the wrong budget.
4/4 complexity points: no headroom. Adding a cache, a CDN or a worker means removing something here or adding an engineer.

The observability point costs GBP 0 on the invoice and about GBP 240/month of engineering attention in the operational model. It is the least defensible point on traffic grounds and the most defensible on failure-detection grounds.

Managed services mean provider lock-in on the platform's deployment model and on the database's backup tooling. Both are escapable with a Postgres dump and a Dockerfile, which is why reversibility is easy rather than moderate.
Photos are permanent with no retention policy, so object storage grows without a plateau.

options.description: The simplest viable option: identical to the selected design with the error tracking and uptime check removed. Three components, one deployable, one datastore technology.
options.reason: Rejected on a fundamental rather than on a measurement, and that distinction is stated deliberately: error tracking is one of the scale-independent fundamentals (alongside tested restore, explicit timeouts and reversible migrations) whose failure is not proportional to traffic, so a small system gets no discount. There is no traffic number that makes this option correct — 0.28 requests/second is exactly the regime in which a silent 500 goes unnoticed for a week. It is also the option that would leave three of the seven triggers below with no source to read them from, and a trigger nobody can read is decoration. It genuinely is one point cheaper in complexity and about GBP 240/month cheaper in the operational model, and if the team already has an aggregated log search they can read daily, this option becomes correct and should be taken.
trade_offs: One point of headroom, which is real and worth having at this team size
Fewer accounts, fewer integrations, one less thing to configure
Failures are discovered by users rather than by the team

options.description: One virtual machine running the application, PostgreSQL, a reverse proxy and photos on the attached block volume, with a cron job shipping database dumps and photos to offsite object storage.
options.reason: The cheapest invoice in the set and the most expensive architecture. Self-hosting the database is 3 points and the app plus proxy is 2, which is 6 against an available budget of 4 — 150% of budget, before any override. In money, the complexity model puts it at roughly GBP 1,460/month all-in against GBP 990 for the selected option, because the GBP 7/month of invoice saving buys about 8 engineer-hours/month of patching, backup verification and restore drilling. The measurement that would reverse this: if the team's own incident and maintenance records show materially under 4 engineer-hours per complexity point per month, or if a dedicated operations engineer joins (which alone raises the budget from 4 to 8), this option comes back into range. The infrastructure budget is not the binding constraint here — GBP 50/month accommodates the selected option comfortably.
trade_offs: Lowest invoice of any option, and no provider lock-in
Full control over versions and tuning
Backups are a cron job the team must test; an untested restore is not a backup
Recovery from a lost volume is a manual rebuild, which does not fit a 4-hour recovery time objective without a drilled runbook

options.description: Two containerised application replicas behind a load balancer, a separately deployed image-processing worker, a managed key-value cache, a CDN in front of object storage, managed relational database, and paid error tracking.
options.reason: This was generated first and failed the budget gate in both dimensions at once — 8 points against 4 available (200%), and GBP 116/month against a GBP 50 budget (232%) — which is what sent the design back to generate the two simpler options above rather than forward to justify this one. Every component in it is individually defensible in the abstract and none of them has a measured problem here: the cache would relieve a database at under 1% utilisation, the CDN would offload 9.4 GB/month, the second replica would take a workload of 0.042 concurrent operations, and the worker would process 9 images a day. The measurement that would change the answer is not one number but four, each of which already has a trigger below: database CPU above 70%, single-key read rate above 10/second, origin egress above 300 GB/month, and app CPU above 70%. Adopting the pieces one at a time as those fire is strictly better than adopting them together now, because by then the real access patterns are known.
trade_offs: Would absorb a 100x traffic increase with no redesign
Rolling deploys with no user-visible restart
Roughly GBP 2,040/month all-in once operational cost is counted, against GBP 990 for the selected option
Eight components for two people to keep patched, monitored and understood

availability.achievable: ~99.5% (roughly 3.6 hours/month), measured as successful requests over total requests
availability.explanation: No availability target was stated, so none is invented — inventing one manufactures requirements and cost. What this architecture actually delivers: a single application instance with platform restart-on-crash, a managed database with a maintenance window, and deploys that are briefly user-visible. Serial dependencies multiply, so the platform (~99.9%) and the database (~99.9%) put a ceiling of about 99.8% on the path before the team's own code, deploys and single-instance restarts are counted; ~99.5% is the honest figure. Reaching 99.9% would need a second instance behind health-checked routing, zero-downtime deploys and database failover, which is roughly 3 more complexity points and 3x the infrastructure cost. If a stakeholder wants 99.9%, that is a different design and a different budget, and it should be a decision rather than an aspiration. Recovery objectives are the part that matters more at this stage: managed point-in-time recovery gives an RPO of minutes against the 24-hour requirement, and a documented, drilled restore is what keeps the 4-hour RTO honest.

triggers.metric: application instance CPU utilisation at peak
triggers.window: sustained 1 hour at daily peak, on 3 consecutive days
triggers.action: Re-run the RPS and concurrency calculations with measured numbers; evaluate vertical resize and profiling before adding a second instance and a load balancer
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation
triggers.notes: 70% rather than 90% because latency is still linear here and there is time to act. Available on the platform dashboard today.

triggers.source: SELECT count(*) FROM users, reviewed at the monthly team check-in
triggers.action: Re-run the whole capacity analysis with measured daily-active share and requests per session; the assumptions this design rests on stop being checked above this point
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation
triggers.notes: This is the sensitivity limit from the RPS analysis, not a round number chosen for comfort: the recommendation is provably unchanged anywhere below it.

triggers.action: Identify the dominant query and check its indexes first; evaluate a read replica or a cache only after query optimisation has been exhausted
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation

triggers.action: Compute the cost of edge offload against current origin egress pricing, and check image derivative sizes and cache headers first — payload reduction is often the larger win than offload
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation
triggers.notes: 300 GB/month at GBP 0.09/GB is GBP 27/month, over half the infrastructure budget. Set below the usual 1 TB threshold precisely because the budget is GBP 50.

triggers.metric: total bytes stored in the photo bucket
triggers.source: object storage provider console, bucket metrics
triggers.action: Decide a retention or tiering policy for photos attached to deleted or unpublished recipes; re-run the storage projection with the measured bytes-per-photo
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation
triggers.notes: 50 GB is roughly 5 years at the projected 9.9 GB/year, or under a year if photo volume is 10x the estimate. Either way it fires with room to plan rather than at the cliff.

triggers.source: provider billing dashboard, reviewed at the monthly team check-in
triggers.action: Break the invoice down by line and identify which capacity assumption moved; re-run the cost calculation before either raising the budget or removing a component
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation

triggers.metric: p95 latency of the recipe search endpoint
triggers.source: error tracking and performance monitoring dashboard
triggers.action: Check the full-text and trigram indexes and the query plan; evaluate a dedicated search engine only if relational search provably cannot meet a stated requirement
triggers.owner: the two developers, on a weekly rotation
triggers.notes: This metric is not emitted today. Instrumenting per-endpoint p95 is a prerequisite of this design, not a follow-up, and it is one of the reasons the observability point is spent.

open_questions: Is there any compliance, data-residency or data-sensitivity constraint that was not mentioned? This is the one-way door in this design: it decides the hosting region and the data-processing terms, and it is far cheaper to answer now than to discover later.

Are recipe photos public once published, or do any of them need per-user access control? Public means they are served straight from the bucket; private means the application enters the image path and both the egress and the compute analysis change.
Does anyone have an availability expectation in mind? None was stated and none has been invented, but ~99.5% with user-visible deploys should be an accepted number rather than a discovered one.

What is the actual daily-active share and photos-per-recipe? These are the two lowest-confidence inputs. Neither changes the recommendation anywhere in its plausible range, but both set the trigger thresholds, and a week of production data would replace both.

Is there a moderation requirement for comments and uploaded photos beyond manual deletion? Automated moderation would introduce an external dependency in the write path, which is a timeout-and-bulkhead question rather than a capacity one.
